title: Word building and spelling
tagline: Swim → swimmer, happy → unhappy: building and spelling new words.
why: New words don't just appear — you build them from ones you already know: add -er for the person who does something, un- for the opposite, -s or -es for more than one. Listening Part 2 and your own writing both punish small spelling slips here.

hook.text: The class is writing the school newsletter. "Is it 'runer' or 'runner'?" asks Mateo. "Runner — double the n!" says Miss Vega. "And a person who teaches is a teacher, right?" "Exactly!"
hook.ask: Runner and teacher both name a person who does something. Can you see the small change from the verb?

diagrams.title: Making a word for the person who does it

rules.rule: Verb ends in -e: just add r
Short vowel + one consonant: double it

diagrams.caption: The -er ending turns an action (swim, teach) into the person who does it (swimmer, teacher).

diagrams.title: Compound nouns: two words, one idea
Plural spelling: -s, -es, -ies

rules.rule: Consonant + y: y becomes i + es

diagrams.caption: Say the plural out loud — if you hear an extra syllable, you probably need -es.

use.point: Nouns from verbs: the person who does it

examples.text: Sofia is a great swimmer — she trains every day.
examples.note: swim → swimmer, the person who swims

examples.text: Mateo wants to be a football player one day.
It's unfair that we have three tests this week.

use.point: Compound nouns: two words, one idea

examples.text: Wait for me at the bus stop.
There's a big football match on Saturday.

examples.note: class + mate = one word, one idea

examples.text: I've got two brothers and one sister.
There are three red buses outside the school.
We visited two cities on our trip.
The babies in that photo are my cousins.

watch_out.why: Add -er to the verb to name the person who does it.
Un- only works with certain adjectives — happy, fair, kind — not every word.

watch_out.wrong: Wait for me at the stop bus.
watch_out.right: Wait for me at the bus stop.
watch_out.why: In English compound nouns, the first word describes the second: bus stop, not stop bus.
Words ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x or -o add -es for the plural.
Consonant + y becomes ies in the plural.

l1.why: Spanish changes the whole word (nadar → nadadora); English usually just adds -er to the verb.
Don't borrow the Spanish prefix in- — English uses un- with happy.
English joins two nouns directly (bus stop); it doesn't use of like Spanish de.
Spanish ciudades doesn't show you the English spelling rule: consonant + y becomes ies.

remember.trick: Verb + er = the doer. Consonant+y? Swap y for ies!
remember.tip: Say the new word out loud — teacher, swimmer, cities — your ear will often tell you if the spelling sounds right.

dialogue.title: Writing the school newsletter
dialogue.context: Sofia, Mateo and Liam write a short article about sports day, and Miss Vega checks their spelling.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good article! But check your spelling — is it buses or busses?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Buses! Bus already ends in -s, so we add -es.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: And what about the person who wins a race?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I wrote that Nadia is unhappy about losing. Is that right?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Yes. And remember: bus stop is two words, but one idea.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Should I write 'two babys' or 'two babies'?

can_do: I can make a noun for a person from a verb, like swim → swimmer.
I can use -ly adverbs and un- to make the opposite of an adjective.
I can spell plurals correctly with -s, -es and -ies, and recognise compound nouns like bus stop.
summary: Add -er to a verb to name the person who does it: swim → swimmer, teach → teacher.
Add -ly to make an adverb, and un- to make the opposite of some adjectives: quick → quickly, happy → unhappy.
Compound nouns join two words into one idea: bus stop, football match.
Plurals add -s, but -es after -s/-sh/-ch/-x/-o, and -ies after a consonant + y.
